malignant.name: Possibly malignant lesion
malignant.what_it_is: The system flagged features it associates with malignant or pre-cancerous lesions, which in this dataset include melanoma, basal cell carcinoma and actinic keratosis. This is a screening signal, not a diagnosis.
common_symptoms: a mole that has changed size, shape or colour
a mole with an uneven shape or edges
a mole with a mix of colours
a mole that is painful, itchy, inflamed, bleeding or crusty
typical_next_steps: See a GP about any mole or skin area that has recently changed
Tell the GP if you or a family member have had skin cancer before
The GP may refer you to a dermatologist; this can be an urgent referral, usually within 2 weeks, which does not by itself mean you have cancer
Finding a melanoma early can make it easier to treat
self_care: Examine your skin about once a month, using a mirror or asking someone to check areas you cannot see, and note anything new or changed
Photograph the lesion so you can compare it over time
Stay out of the sun during the hottest part of the day, generally 11am to 3pm
Use sunscreen of at least SPF 30 with 4-star UVA protection, applied generously and reapplied after swimming
Cover up with loose clothing, a wide-brimmed hat and sunglasses
Never let your skin burn, and avoid sunbeds
Remember UV passes through cloud, so protection matters on overcast days too
malignant.source: NHS Melanoma skin cancer symptoms (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/melanoma-skin-cancer/symptoms); Hull University Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust, Skin and nodal self-examination (https://hey.nhs.uk/patient-leaflet/skin-nodal-self-examination)

benign.name: Likely benign lesion
benign.what_it_is: The system did not flag features it associates with malignancy. In this dataset, benign lesions include ordinary moles (melanocytic nevi), benign keratoses and dermatofibromas.
typical_next_steps: A 'benign' result does not rule out skin cancer; this system is tuned for screening and still misses some malignant lesions
See a GP if the lesion changes size, shape or colour, or becomes painful, itchy, inflamed, bleeding or crusty
See a GP about any new or unusual mark on your skin that has not gone away after a few weeks
self_care: Check your moles regularly for change; most moles are harmless but it is worth knowing what is normal for you
Photograph the lesion now so you have a reference point for comparison later
Protect moles from sun damage: cover up, wear a hat if moles are on your face, and use SPF 30 or higher
Take extra care in the sun if you have many moles or pale skin
benign.source: NHS Moles (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/moles/); NHS Melanoma skin cancer symptoms (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/melanoma-skin-cancer/symptoms)

vascular.name: Vascular lesion
vascular.what_it_is: A skin lesion made up of blood vessels, such as an angioma. These are generally benign.
typical_next_steps: See a GP if the lesion is new, changing, bleeding, or causing you concern
As with any skin lesion, a GP or dermatologist should confirm what it is
self_care: Avoid scratching or picking at the lesion, which can cause bleeding
Photograph it so you can tell whether it changes over time
Continue normal sun protection: cover up, use SPF 30 or higher, and avoid sunbeds
See a GP if it starts bleeding repeatedly or grows noticeably
